9: \section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
10: 
11: The closest methods differ primarily in where they freeze features and how they
12: represent uncertainty.  That distinction matters here because a covariance
13: built from stored features answers a different question from one that replays
14: every observation at the current parameter.
15: 
16: \paragraph{Positive-cone metric geometry.}
17: \citet{thompson1963certain} introduced the part metric now commonly called the
18: Thompson metric on ordered cones.  \citet{nussbaum1994finsler} developed its
19: Finsler structure and applications.  On the positive-definite cone, the
20: normalized operator norm
21: $\|V^{-1/2}\dot V V^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}$ is the corresponding tangent norm.
22: Our contribution is not this geometry or its path-to-endpoint comparison.  We
23: instantiate it as an operational confidence-transport device linking frozen
24: bandit confidence, current replayed GGN/Fisher curvature, approximate operators,
25: and certified solver widths.
26: 
27: \paragraph{Misspecified linear confidence.}
28: \citet[Appendix~E]{lattimore2020learning} analyze LinUCB with round-dependent
29: feature sets and an explicit bonus for bounded misspecification.
30: Our pseudo-responses in \Cref{eq:pseudo-response-new} reduce the nonlinear
31: observations to predictable linear regression with a Taylor remainder and
32: misspecification error.  The corrected center then adds the current affine
33: offset.  Its confidence argument combines standard self-normalized regression
34: confidence with deterministic bias bounds; we do not claim a new generic
35: misspecified-linear confidence method.  The additional issue studied here is
36: how to certify the use of current replayed curvature, approximate operators,
37: and computed widths for this reference confidence model.
38: 
39: \paragraph{Weighted Gram comparisons.}
40: Weighted least-squares Grams also appear in the experimental-design analysis of
41: \citet{lattimore2020learning}.  Our scaled-tanh specialization compares two
42: positive weightings of fixed feature directions through termwise PSD bounds
43: (\Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights}).  The reward model stays fixed while
44: relinearization changes the weights.  We use this elementary comparison as an
45: operational endpoint certificate within the confidence-transport interface;
46: nonstationary reward models require a separate statistical analysis.
47: 
48: \paragraph{Neural contextual bandits.}
49: LinUCB \citep{abbasi2011improved} and Thompson sampling
50: \citep{thompson1933likelihood,agrawal2013thompson} provide the statistical
51: backbone for many neural extensions.  In their stated algorithms, NeuralUCB
52: \citep{zhou2020neural} and NeuralTS \citep{zhang2021neural} add a gradient
53: feature to the covariance when its observation arrives; they do not replay the
54: entire history at each new parameter.  \citet{kassraie2022neural} separate a
55: kernelized NTK reference from a trained-network mean with initialization-time
56: uncertainty features, and prove sublinear regret for the SupNN-UCB variant under
57: NTK-RKHS, sufficient-exploration, and network-width assumptions.
58: \citet{salgia2023provably}
59: controls adaptivity through grouped histories and a finite-network-to-NTK
60: confidence argument.  \citet{deb2024contextual} take a different route through
61: online neural regression and contextual-bandit reductions.  These results do
62: not lack proofs because their covariance differs from ours; they answer
63: different questions.  We analyze the additional case in which every historical
64: Jacobian is replayed at the current parameter.  The theorem allows certified
65: operator and solve approximations; the experiment uses dense current metrics
66: and direct Cholesky solves.
67: 
68: The NeuralLinear method maintains Bayesian linear uncertainty in learned
69: final-layer features \citep{riquelme2018deep}; the methods of
70: \citet{xu2022shallow} and \citet{bui2025variance} instead use UCB-style linear
71: exploration over learned deep representations.  Recomputing those last-layer
72: representations is not the same as transporting confidence to a full-parameter
73: GGN.  The present theorem asks what certificates justify that transport; it
74: does not provide a general analysis of neural-linear representation learning.
75: 
76: \paragraph{Online Bayesian and EKF-style neural bandits.}
77: \citet{duranmartin2022efficient} apply extended Kalman filter (EKF)
78: updates in a learned or random low-dimensional affine parameter subspace.
79: They maintain a dense or diagonal covariance in that subspace, inducing a
80: low-rank covariance over parameters spanning all network layers, with memory
81: independent of the number of rounds.  This differs from applying exact
82: curvature--vector products in the full parameter space.
83: More directly, \citet{chang2023lowrank} maintain a diagonal-plus-low-rank
84: approximation to the full-parameter posterior precision through recursive EKF
85: and online-SVD updates, and use it for Thompson sampling in an MNIST contextual
86: bandit.  Their LO-FI method is a one-pass compressed-posterior approach with
87: fixed-rank cost linear in parameter count and no replay of past data.  Our
88: transported-UCB analysis instead relates current replayed curvature to a
89: separate frozen-feature confidence metric.  Certified approximate operators and
90: solver widths enter through explicit comparison factors.  The dense audit
91: evaluates neither compressed operators nor CG, and establishes no practical
92: advantage over LO-FI.
93: 
94: \paragraph{Linearized networks and Laplace approximations.}
95: \citet{maddox2021fast} linearize once around a trained network and use implicit
96: Jacobian/Fisher products with CG for predictive inference.  Their construction
97: is a computational antecedent for matrix-free widths, but the reference
98: linearization is fixed rather than replayed online.  The Laplace approximation
99: places a local Gaussian posterior around a MAP solution with covariance defined
100: by inverse curvature \citep{mackay1992practical}.  Last-layer Laplace fixes the
101: backbone, omitting backbone-weight uncertainty by construction
102: \citep{kristiadi2020being}.  \citet{daxberger2021laplace} systematize all-weight,
103: subnetwork, and last-layer variants with full, low-rank, Kronecker-factored, or
104: diagonal curvature; structured all-layer variants use Kronecker-factored
105: curvature \citep{ritter2018scalable,martens2015optimizing}.  Our concern is
106: instead the sequential validity of a UCB score when the current relinearized
107: operator differs from the predictable confidence Gram.
108: 
109: \paragraph{Sampling-based full-parameter exploration.}
110: Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson sampling (LMC-TS) \citep{xu2022langevin}
111: explores with approximate samples of a loss-defined parameter posterior,
112: obtained by noisy gradient steps on the regularized loss without materializing
113: a covariance matrix.  Its regret guarantee is for linear
114: contextual bandits; its neural-bandit evidence is empirical.
115: LMC-TS requires control of its per-round sampling approximation.  Our
116: optimism-based theorem instead requires certificates for metric transport,
117: operator distortion, and the width used by action selection.  These are
118: different statistical obligations; our dense audit does not compare their
119: computational cost or empirical performance.
120: \paragraph{Scope of efficient nonlinear exploration.}
121: The methods above obtain efficiency through different statistical objects:
122: fixed NTK features, grouped data, regression reductions, or learned last-layer
123: representations.  Our conditional theorem addresses scores based on a specific
124: current full-parameter GGN/Fisher operator.  It
125: exposes what that choice requires: transport from collection-time confidence,
126: operator distortion, and solver error.  It does not imply that this route is
127: computationally preferable to the alternatives.
128: 
129: \paragraph{Spectral sketching for linear bandits.}
130: \citet{kuzborskij2019efficient} analyze linear bandits where the Gram
131: matrix is replaced by a Frequent Directions sketch, deriving regret
132: bounds that depend on the spectral approximation quality.  They already note
133: that SOFUL may incur linear regret when the spectrum has heavy tails.
134: The two-sided comparison in \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} uses the same conceptual
135: lever to relate an applied operator to exact current curvature.  A separate path
136: certificate relates that curvature to the frozen-feature confidence metric,
137: and a solver certificate controls the computed width.  We claim no novelty for
138: the sandwich-to-regret reduction itself and do not evaluate a sketched operator.
139: 
140: \paragraph{Curvature--vector products and influence functions.}
141: Pearlmutter's algorithm \citep{pearlmutter1994fast} computes exact
142: Hessian--vector products; the analogous GGN--vector product has the same
143: Jacobian-transpose-times-Jacobian-times-vector structure
144: \citep{schraudolph2002fast}.
145: Influence functions
146: \citep{koh2017understanding} use inverse-curvature--vector products to
147: attribute predictions to training points.  A CG-based realization of our solver
148: interface would use the same implicit-solve primitive.  The present experiment
149: uses direct dense solves and makes no matrix-free scalability claim.
150: 
151: \paragraph{Optimal experimental design.}
152: Information-theoretic exploration objectives---such as maximizing
153: $\log\det(\bVbar_t)$ or minimizing the trace of~$\bVbar_t^{-1}$---connect
154: bandit exploration to the classical D-optimal and A-optimal design
155: criteria \citep{valko2013finite}.  Stochastic trace and log-determinant
156: estimators provide related matrix-free tools \citep{ubaru2017fast}.  Here the
157: frozen log-determinant appears in the regret analysis; the audited policy
158: selects actions by its UCB score and does not implement these estimators.
